toc.title: "Getting into my body was my game changer"
"It's just you. Just me. I like me."

blocks.p: I made the case that it's just you. There are no parts. There's no shadow. There's no reparenting, no ego, no this and that. It's just you. I laid out that these concepts can be helpful, and I'll say that over and over again. Yes, they can be helpful. I'm not trying to take that away from you. Maybe I kind of am. But I also don't think they're necessary.

I got a number of responses, on Instagram and by email, and everyone was really cool about it. Some people respectfully disagreed. Some expressed appreciation and agreed. Some were somewhere in the middle and were just interested in the ideas. Here I want to share some of the ones that were in support of the idea, because I want to make these ideas more normalized. No one else is really thinking and talking like this in the mental health arena, from what I can tell. The ones that disagreed deserve their own time, so I'm not letting myself off the hook.

blocks.h: "Getting into my body was my game changer"

blocks.p: One person wrote:

"So true. Talking about my parts, shadows, whatever, didn't help me in any way. It just made things complicated and kept me in my head analyzing while emotions showed up. I couldn't integrate them. Getting into my body, learning how to really sense myself through the day without labeling was my game changer."
I'm super happy they found what's working for them. The parts thing, the shadows thing, the whatever thing: these can be helpful. They're not for everybody, and I don't think they're necessary.
Another wrote:

"These are constructs to help us conceptualize ourselves to achieve a measure of emotional balance, et cetera. And yes, ultimately, it is just us. I think of ego as a concept, a possible choice, not an intrinsic part of me."

That's exactly what it is. These are constructs, or concepts, which is the word I used, to help us conceptualize ourselves and achieve a measure of emotional balance. They're top-down ways of thinking that may help contain or reduce dysregulation.

From Polyvagal Theory, we're really focused on autonomic dysregulation and how it shows up in your thoughts, your behaviors, your impulses, and your sensations. These top-down narratives, reframes, and psychological concepts are a conceptualization. At a minimum, I think the benefit is that they help reduce activation. At a maximum, from what I can see, they may help people get a step closer to their felt sense, or more directly to it. Again, I don't think they're necessary, but for some people they may be very, very helpful. If that's you, I'm happy for you.
I like this one a lot, because it adds something:

"Love this. Concepts are helpful until they're not. For me, it's about fluidity and flexibility to put down what's not working when it's not working, and pick it back up if it works again, and continuing on with that."

I like that idea a lot: these concepts can be tools we pick up and use when we need them. If that works for you, I'm very much on board. I have no issue with you using them. But realize that these are ideas. It's really important to know what they are and what they are not. They are not you, because it's just you.

One longer email really touched me in a different way. I get a lot of love and support from people, and people write to me expressing that they're grateful, and that means a lot to me. But this one meant a lot in a different way.

Saying it's just you is not revolutionary. It seems pretty common sense. But it kind of is revolutionary, because nobody in the psychology realm or the therapy realm talks that way. If they think it, they don't say it, and that was me for quite a while. I kept it to myself. I don't want it to be revolutionary. I want it to be clearly understood for what it is.

They opened with, "I feel the need to agree that of course you are not my therapist. I have one. It's cool." I'm really glad they opened with that. If you can't tell by now, I have a lot of anxiety and cautiousness around boundaries and my license, and making sure I can keep doing my profession, which I love. So I get a little antsy when it comes to content creation.
Then they wrote, "I loved seeing and hearing your thoughts about psychological concepts. In fact, it was validating to hear what you had to say."
I'm pumping my fist right now like I just threw a touchdown.
"I agree that they can be helpful in giving a person an expansive metaphor to work with..."
Right there, we're on the same page. They're a tool. You can use them for top-down regulation. Awesome.
"...but in the online arena, they often seem to be mere buzzwords thrown out to entice you to purchase a self-help program."

I think they're right about this. I do want to say I don't think these ideas inherently exist to take advantage of people. But it absolutely could happen, especially with people who are desperate for change. That might be you. The person who's desperate for change will latch onto whatever seems to be helpful, and I don't blame them. That tells me it's even more important that we're very clear about what these concepts are and what they are not. They are not real. These are ideas.
They continued:

"I've spent years thinking I was the problem in my 'complicated marriage' and my 'difficult' relationship with my parents. Spoiler alert: I am not. The emotional abuse of my childhood set me up to accept behavior from my husband that is not okay. I have read tons of self-help books, taken thirty-day challenges, even purchased one recovery program. I followed people on social media who claimed a person must do 'shadow work' to overcome trauma (fine, how do I do that?), or who claimed a person must heal their inner child (sounds good, how the hell do I do that?)."
There's no child inside of you, by the way, people. I had to interject that.

Again, I don't think these things are necessarily bad, and I don't think someone who espouses these ideas is necessarily out to take advantage of you. But I think we need to be aware, and really scrutinize who we're listening to. I invite you to do the same thing with me. If I'm not coming at this with integrity, if what I'm saying doesn't make sense, if I'm not backing up my claims or explaining what I'm telling you, you probably should stop listening to me. If I'm just spouting ideas and saying, "This is the way it is, and here's a course," that's not super helpful.

I do the best I can to provide free information that's clear, structured, and makes sense, even with complex ideas. Yes, I sell stuff as well. I need to make a living, and I have goals for myself and my family.

"The thing is, they never tell you anything specific about how to do those things that isn't 'sit with your feelings' (yeah, you can totally re-traumatize yourself if you don't know what that means, LOL), or journal, meditate, et cetera. The same things that every other modality seems to suggest."

Maybe that's a gauge: how specific are they being? They're teaching concepts, but how specific is it? I think there's a marketing mindset out there where you keep things general, and then get people to buy the course where you sell the real clarity or answers.

And she's absolutely right. If you just jump into this stuff, it's possible to re-traumatize yourself. If you're expecting to get help by just sitting and journaling about the horrible things that happened to you, or the things you didn't receive, you could be setting yourself up for re-traumatization. You could be reinforcing your own stuck defensive state without realizing it, and obviously without wanting to.

"I am still working through accepting that I've been in one sort of abusive relationship or another for my entire life, and then working out what I'm going to do from here. I've made HELLA progress in the last six months. All those psychological concepts you talked about didn't really help me at all. The things that actually did help me were:"

ol: "My therapist saying, in regard to my marriage, 'Maybe the problem isn't you.' Also, other things that she says. She's great."

blocks.p: So number one is having a good therapist, someone she feels a connection with, and that therapist saying those five words. I'm not saying therapists have magic words to give you, or that these five words have any inherent therapeutic properties. I'm not saying you should buy a course called Maybe the Problem Isn't You. I'm saying that sentence meant a lot to this person, and it had more of an impact than all those psychological concepts.

ol: "Polyvagal Theory. I had been a wreck for so long that I thought the goal was to better compartmentalize my anxiety/depression so that I could keep being productive. Safe and Social was a revelation. Learning that much of my anxiety, depression, and shutdown could directly be traced to events where I felt threatened, and that it was a biological process and not a shameful weakness. WHOA. Huge. Because the shutdowns fueled my shame, which fueled more shutdown. Being able to remove the shame from that hellish feedback loop has been revolutionary."

blocks.p: Learning Polyvagal Theory gave her a new top-down understanding. Not a concept: foundational knowledge.

ol: "Finding an online support group for people in a long-term relationship with BPD. Yes, I know I can't diagnose him, my therapist can't diagnose him, et cetera. But to find a group of ridiculously supportive people who all share eerily similar experiences has been freaking amazing."

blocks.p: I have to reiterate: I'm not telling you to drop your shadow work. If it's helpful and you like it, have at it. I'm not saying do these three things and you're all set. Actually, I'm not saying it at all. I'm reading it. This person said these things were more helpful than the psychological concepts. It's not for everybody. That's obvious. It's also not real. It's an idea, and I want to keep reinforcing that. These are ideas you either buy into or you don't.

One person on Instagram responded to a post where I said these psychological concepts are not real. It looks like they deleted the comment, which is unfortunate. They wrote that these concepts are no less real than Polyvagal Theory, and that me saying so was actually my shadow talking. Or no, it was one of my parts talking. See, I'm already getting confused.

So here's an example where I'm saying, "This doesn't work for me. I'm not interested in these ideas. I don't buy into it." And for the person who read that, it was evidence that the ideas were true. Me saying I don't buy into it actually reinforced the ideas for them. I find that fascinating.
The letter wrapped up:

"Anyway, I recently commented in that group that we're all heading in roughly the same direction, but we each need different tools to get there. Part of being in the group is seeing what everyone else has in their tool belt and figuring out which tools work for you."

If a psychological concept works for you as a tool, have at it. I think it's a problem if you see everything through that lens. I think it's a problem if someone saying "I don't want to be a part of this" becomes evidence that your ideas are more true. It has a place, like that earlier comment about fluidity and flexibility: put it down when it's not working, and pick it back up if it works again. Use what's in your tool belt, run with it until it's burned out or you're ready for something else.

I do think we have a shared destination. Biologically, we have this impulse to be self-regulated, to provide co-regulation, to connect with each other, to be able to exist in play and in stillness. What it looks like for you to get there is different from me. You might like parts work. Awesome. I don't.

Part of how I want to help people who are interested in the way I think is to spread a different idea: you don't need these. You have everything you need within you. You can disagree with that and say, "No, Justin, I don't," and I believe you. That's fine. But I'm saying ultimately we have what we need. I don't use these ideas personally, and I don't use them in therapy. I've worked with some severely traumatized people from all walks of life, and I've never used metaphors to that extent at all. So I don't think they're necessary. They can be helpful, yes.

blocks.h: "It's just you. Just me. I like me."

blocks.p: They ended:

"So many of the psychological concepts you talked about just did not resonate with me. For me, they seem like just one more fad diet of the month. It's a gigantic relief to hear someone say, 'It's just you.' Just me. I like me. I like feeling safe and social. I like collecting things that make me feel that way, even if some days are impossible or it's difficult to hold onto that safe feeling. I like the simplicity of this. No complicated metaphors and concepts, just find who, what, where makes you feel safe and social. Practice. Some days are still going to suck, but it gets easier. Bam."

That's a really great summary, and I don't disagree with any of it. It seems like this person and I work similarly. When something is simple and clear and structured and straight to the point, it clicks. Something within me lights up. No, it's not a part. It's me. I feel lit up. I feel a sensation of connection. I feel excitement. I have a sensation in my brain like magnets clicking together, this idea and that idea, and it's like, yes. It's an experience, a sensation. It's not a part. Maybe parts connect to sensations and experience, fine. But I'm having a true experience, and I really like that simplicity. It's more direct, in my opinion.

That works for me, and it seems to work for this person too. Maybe this way of thinking works for you. I want to build it, because I don't see it anywhere else. Maybe it's out there. I don't spend a ton of time perusing other people's content. But I don't see it in any obvious way. What seems popular is the psychological concepts. So I want to create a dialogue, or at least a monologue on my end, about something different: something clearer, more to the point, simple, and structured.
